draft.title: The stance of monetary policy
card: The stance of monetary policy describes whether interest rates are pushing spending and activity up, pulling them down, or doing neither. It is judged against the neutral rate.
The neutral rate is the interest rate that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy. It cannot be seen directly, so it is estimated.
rates are below neutral. Borrowing is cheaper, so spending and economic activity tend to rise.

rates are above neutral. Borrowing is dearer, so spending and economic activity tend to slow. Neutral means rates are close to the neutral rate. Recent changes in the cash rate show which way the RBA leans.
draft.remember: Compare rates with neutral: below is expansionary, above is contractionary.

a.q: The RBA estimates the neutral rate at 3%. The cash rate is 1.5%. What is the stance of monetary policy?
opts: Expansionary, as rates are below neutral
Contractionary, as rates are below neutral
Expansionary, as rates are above neutral
Neutral, as rates are low
a.why: The cash rate is below the neutral rate, so borrowing is cheaper and policy is expansionary. A low rate alone does not make policy neutral. Neutral means close to the neutral rate.
a.clue: Compare the cash rate with the neutral rate, not with zero.

b.q: Over a year, the RBA raises the cash rate from 0.1% to 3.1%. Neutral is estimated at about 3.5%. Which statement is best supported?
opts: Policy is still expansionary, but less so than before
Policy has become contractionary, as rates have risen
Policy is now neutral, as rates are close to neutral
Policy is expansionary, as rates have been raised
b.why: Rates rose, but they are still below the neutral estimate, so policy remains expansionary, only less so. The tempting answer is contractionary, which confuses a rising rate with a rate above neutral. The stance depends on the level compared with neutral.
b.clue: Rising rates are not the same as rates above neutral.

a.best: Expansionary, as rates are below neutral

b.best: Policy is still expansionary, but less so than before
also_right: Policy is now neutral, as rates are close to neutral

problems.detail: The card defines neutral as rates 'close to the neutral rate' and says neutral is only an estimate. A cash rate of 3.1% against an estimate of 'about 3.5%' could fairly be called close to neutral, so 'Policy is now neutral' is defensible. Widen the gap (for example 2.1% against 3.5%) or make the estimate firmer.

The definition of neutral and the line 'Recent changes in the cash rate show which way the RBA leans' are packed into the contractionary bullet. This blurs the three stances. The 'which way the RBA leans' line, read alone, could also seem to support the wrong option 'contractionary, as rates have risen' in question b. Give neutral its own bullet, and make clear that the stance depends on the level against neutral, while recent changes show the direction.

proposal.title: The stance of monetary policy
card: The neutral rate is the cash rate that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy. It cannot be seen directly, so it is estimated.
The stance of monetary policy depends on the level of the cash rate compared with neutral. Below neutral is expansionary, above is contractionary, and close to neutral is neutral.
Expansionary policy makes borrowing cheaper, so spending and activity tend to rise. Contractionary policy makes borrowing dearer, so spending and activity tend to slow.
Recent changes in the cash rate show which way the RBA is leaning. Raising rates while they are still well below neutral tightens policy, but it stays expansionary.
proposal.remember: The level against neutral gives the stance. Recent changes give the direction.
